title: ‘The Angry Birds Movie 3’ Unpacked by VFX Supervisor, Including Red’s Redesign and Character-Effects Automation: ’He’s Similar by Choice’
description: The red-feathered hero of “The Angry Birds Movie 3” looks reassuringly familiar, but DNEG Animation had to rebuild much of him to bring the franchi
body:
The red-feathered hero of “The Angry Birds Movie 3” looks reassuringly familiar, but DNEG Animation had to rebuild much of him to bring the franchise back to theaters. And as the studio reconstructed Red’s fur, facial rig and expressions, it also developed a system that ultimately automated character-effects work on roughly 75% of the film’s shots.

	“He’s similar by choice,” VFX supervisor Patrick Harboun said at View Conference in Turin on Friday.
	

	The upcoming Paramount release, directed by John Rice, reunites Jason Sudeikis’ Red with Silver, voiced by Rachel Bloom, as they navigate parenthood alongside their latest adventure. DNEG takes over animation duties from the Sony Pictures Animation productions behind the first two films.


	The technical handover was anything but straightforward. In fact, proprietary grooming, rigging and surfacing tools used on the predecessors could not simply be transferred to DNEG’s pipeline. “We had to start from this. A plucked chicken version of Red,” Harboun joked, displaying a bare digital model. Even its underlying geometry needed reworking before the team could reconstruct its feathers.

	The result deliberately avoided a radical makeover. Red’s plumage became slightly softer, while his eyes and beak gained firmer, more toy-like surfaces. “Once an IP becomes popular, it kind of belongs to the fans, and we have to respect that,” Harboun said. “We can’t just add our own spin just to give our mark.”

	The studio scrutinized the earlier movies frame by frame. “We analyzed the past movies to find the unwritten rules of animation,” he explained. Animators cataloged the angles of Red’s beak, the geometry of his narrowed eyes and the boundaries beyond which a stretched expression stopped feeling like Red. The lessons became a style guide and a reusable library of facial expressions.
	

	There was more room for experimentation with over 20 new characters, including Red and Silver’s children: aspiring athlete Glider, voiced by Walker Scobell; temperamental June, played by Emma Myers; and baby Olly, voiced by Psalm West. The family also has a pet spider named Fuzzy, voiced by James Austin Johnson. “The goal was to make a spider that even an arachnophobe would love,” Harboun said.

	Olly created a distinctive technical challenge because his glasses effectively serve as animated eyes, complete with moving eyelids and brows. DNEG’s solution, nicknamed “Pancake Eyes,” involved duplicating and flattening portions of the baby’s facial rig behind the lenses, then restoring curvature and allowing the expressions to respond to the character’s exaggerated squash-and-stretch movement.

	The biggest efficiency gain came through a performance-effects process building on DNEG’s earlier work for “The Garfield Movie.” Following approval of a character’s animation, the system automatically simulated selected effects on fur, feathers and deformation, rendered a preview and identified shots requiring bespoke artist attention. As the crew encountered new problems, they improved reusable templates for each character.

	“It’s not machine learning, it’s human learning,” Harboun underlined, stressing that artists maintained those templates. Early in production, around 25% of shots could pass through the automated process; by later stages, that figure had risen to 75%. “This frees up a lot of artists for hero work,” he explained. The percentage applies to character-effects processing, not to shots being animated or completed without artists.

	Other inventions included a secondary, normally invisible layer of fur that appears when characters stretch, preventing bald patches, and one-click tools for building ropes, hay and props that animators could manipulate independently, without repeatedly calling on other departments.

	Production designer Jeanie Chang’s saturated tropical palette posed another challenge. Lighting references were painted directly over layout images so artists could match intended compositions, but differently colored characters still required individual lighting adjustments within the same scene. “In every given situation, Red always needs to be red,” Harboun said.
	

	The film also expands Bird Island with Pigtropolis, a city for its pig residents. Harboun revealed that the opening sequence was changed from night to day late in production. He encouraged audiences to seek out the 3D version when the film opens Dec. 23: “I’m usually not a fan of 3D, but I really recommend that you check out the 3D version.”

	For Harboun, such innovations only work when they reinforce what audiences already recognize. The characters may have been rebuilt and their workflows reinvented, but their familiar identities remain the foundation.

schema.headline: ‘The Angry Birds Movie 3’ Unpacked by VFX Supervisor, Including Red’s Redesign and Character-Effects Automation: ’He’s Similar by Choice’

title: Mahershala Ali Cries Recalling ‘Moonlight’ Scene, Keeps Quiet on ‘Spider-Verse’ at London Talk: ‘I’ve Got to Be Careful’
description: Mahershala Ali broke down in tears on stage at the BFI London Film Festival on Saturday as he recalled the young boy at the heart of “Moonlight.”
body:
Mahershala Ali broke down in tears on stage at the BFI London Film Festival on Saturday as he recalled the young boy at the heart of “Moonlight.” 

	The Barry Jenkins drama won him one of his two Oscars and recently marked its 10th anniversary.

	During a Screen Talk hosted by Amon Warmann, Ali was discussing the dinner-table scene in which young Chiron asks Juan, the drug dealer Ali plays, whether he sells drugs. “You see this like crisis for this young boy who’s already in crisis,” he said. “It’s really heartbreaking.”
	

	When Warmann asked what accounted for the film’s enduring power, Ali paused, overcome with emotion and wiping away tears. “Sorry, just need a second,” he said.


	“Any time people put flesh on the bones of those who haven’t been seen or had their moment, I think it’s important,” he said once he had composed himself. “I think ‘Moonlight’ was able to make those characters people… make it personal.”

	To play Juan, Ali drew on a man he had known all his life, an uncle-like figure he had grown up playing basketball with who also worked as a substitute teacher. The man was arrested and sent to prison while Ali was in college, which left the actor stunned.

	“I thought of him a lot in the making of the film because of how human everyone was in my environment and in my upbringing,” Ali said.

	He was candid about the backlash that followed “Green Book,” in which he played pianist Don Shirley opposite Viggo Mortensen. It was his first role of that magnitude, and the backlash included the controversy over what Shirley’s family had and hadn’t sanctioned.
	

	“I still stand by it. I stand by the work,” Ali said, adding that he also stands by “the experience as a whole, and what it taught me.”

	Ali, who won his second Oscar for the role, described going from feeling like a golden boy to wondering what he had done wrong. “I think I’m just sensitive in general, you know what I mean? So it definitely like had its impact, like for sure,” he said, adding that he was grateful for the exposure. “Like swords are folded in the fire, you know?”

	Of his back-to-back Oscar wins, Ali said: “I felt a sense of accomplishment, which is not fulfillment.” He keeps the statuettes in a cabinet, out of his sight line, so he could get back to work.

	Ali voices Aaron Davis in the animated “Spider-Verse” films, including a version of the character from another universe who appears at the end of “Across the Spider-Verse” and returns in “Beyond the Spider-Verse.” Asked how he tells the two apart, he said: “I don’t want to give anything away or spoil anything, I’ve got to be careful.” Pressed on whether he had finished recording, he joked: “I might not even be in it, man! I don’t know, man! I don’t know!”

	He was more forthcoming about the process. Actors are filmed in the booth, and their improvised moments often make it into the finished film, sometimes prompting rewrites and extra recording sessions. “I think that’s why, honestly, the animation films will hold up better than live-action films,” Ali said.

	The actor went straight from “Green Book” into “True Detective,” with only a week or two off, to play detective Wayne Hays across three timelines. Playing the older Hays meant 80-hour weeks, with four hours in the makeup chair from 3:30 a.m. The shoot ran seven months, and his daughter was a year old at the time.

	“I just think about how I almost went crazy doing that part,” he said.

	Two of Ali’s films are screening at the festival. He voices bandit leader Brendan in the animated “Wildwood.” In action thriller “Your Mother, Your Mother, Your Mother,” he plays Latif, a devout Muslim father and contract killer, and had three or four days to learn the fight choreography.

	“It’s really more like dance than what people realize,” he said.
	

	On playing a Black Muslim father, Ali said: “I don’t feel like Black fathers have the dimensionality that I would love for them to have.”

	Now at work on the HBO series “Task” with Mark Ruffalo, Ali said he feels “exhausted for the right reasons” and “tired in the right way.”

	“So that’s why I feel like I’m just getting started,” he said.

schema.headline: Mahershala Ali Cries Recalling ‘Moonlight’ Scene, Keeps Quiet on ‘Spider-Verse’ at London Talk: ‘I’ve Got to Be Careful’

title: Joel Coen Talks Studio Consolidation –  ‘Competition Is What Produces Opportunities for Different Kinds of Movies’ – and Teases Reunion Film With Brother Ethan
description: The Coen brothers could be heading back to their hometown in Minneapolis for a reunion movie eight years after their last joint film, “The Ballad o
body:
The Coen brothers could be heading back to their hometown in Minneapolis for a reunion movie eight years after their last joint film, “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs.”

	While at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival, where they received a career tribute, Joel and Ethan Coen revealed they have several projects in the pipeline set in Minneapolis, where they previously shot “Fargo” in 1996 and “A Serious Man” in 2009. 


	“We haven’t discussed it in terms of plot or narrative or what kind of movie. But we’ve discussed going back because there are certain crew people we missed,” said Ethan, sitting alongside Joel, Lumiere festival chief Thierry Fremaux (who also heads Cannes), and film journalist Didier Allouche.
	

	“Yes, there are a couple of other stories that we’ve thought about that would take place in Minneapolis, which is where we come from. So we’ll see if they haven’t sort of germinated to the point where we would go, you know, that’s what we’re going to do next, or we’re even going to definitely do,” said Joel Coen. 

	Joel was responding to a challenge from Oscar-winning actor Frances McDormand, his wife of 42 years, who had playfully urged them on stage at the Lumiere ceremony to complete the unofficial trilogy that began with “Fargo” and “A Serious Man.” “I think Fran wants to see it. We’ll see if we can accommodate her,” Joel joked.

	Since Netflix’s “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs,” Joel went on to direct “The Tragedy of Macbeth,” starring McDormand and Denzel Washington, while Ethan made “Drive-Away Dolls” and “Honey Don’t!,” both co-written with his wife and longtime collaborator Tricia Cooke.
	

	But the brothers said they have continued writing together and have several unproduced scripts. “We’ve written a lot of scripts that we’ve never made,” Ethan said. Joel then joked that “one of which we could not find on the computer.” 

	“One of the Minneapolis stories we were talking about had a main part intended for an actor who has since died. So we’re thinking, well, we’re not sure that’s going to work. That’s a consequence of aging,” Ethan said. 

	They also wrote a new script together while each was working on a separate film, but it now feels outdated to them. “It deals with issues in the culture that we’ve sort of moved on from, or the culture has moved on from. It feels more like a period movie now. Should we make it or shouldn’t we?” he said. “Ethan suggested they could simply introduce the film with a title card reading, ‘Sometime during the Obama administration.’ It’s almost now, but it’s not now anymore.”

	Yet, the brothers aren’t looking to get overly political, even if their films are often satires.  “Things like the political situation in the United States are a kind of background against which you tell stories. But the idea of literalizing it in terms of Trump specifically is probably not in our wheelhouse, in terms of how we think about a story,” Joel said. 

	“We don’t really think of any of our movies as commenting on America currently, or commenting on anything outside the story itself. Audiences are entitled to take our movies any way they want. Making those comparisons may be totally appropriate for an audience, but we literally don’t think about it that way,” Ethan said. 

	The Coens also weighed in on the changing film business, including the role of streaming platforms, which have backed some of their recent projects. Netflix produced and released “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs,” while Joel’s “The Tragedy of Macbeth” was released theatrically by A24 before streaming on Apple TV+.

	Asked about the impact of streaming on cinema, the brothers said they had mixed feelings, pointing out that their own careers had benefited from the rise of home video in the 1980s, when studios were more willing to finance independent films because they had additional ways of making money.

	“In a strange way, we owe our careers to the fact that there were other formats for distribution, and they happened to be home video formats,” Joel said, adding that it would be “disingenuous” for them to oppose new distribution platforms outright.
	

	But Joel also defended the theatrical experience, echoing his comments during the masterclass he took part with Ethan in Lyon on Friday. The worst thing you can get is somebody saying, ‘I loved your movie. I saw it on an airplane.’ It’s very discouraging,” Joel said. “This festival is all about sitting in a big room with a lot of people in the dark watching it. There’s no substitute for that. And so every filmmaker, I think, feels that way.”

	He argued streamers themselves are starting to recognize the importance of theatrical releases again. “I actually think there’s a point now in which the streaming services are recognizing again the value of theatrical distribution, and my hope is that that will continue and everyone will see it as a net advantage,” Joel noted. 

	Asked about AI, Joel dismissed the idea that AI could take over screenwriting as “nonsense,’ but was critical of the “computer-generated images” that AI is helping create, even if helps filmmakers creating images and worlds that would otherwise be impossible.

	“In a way, everything’s becoming a cartoon. Every movie is an animated movie, or it’s becoming more and more like that, especially because of things like AI and effects that are done in a computer,” he said. 

	Joel cited their 1990 film “Miller’s Crossing,” recalling how the opening shot of a hat blowing through the woods was created using thin wires manipulated by crew members outside the frame.

	“There’s no one on earth that would do it that way now. It would be animated, and I’m quite certain that it would not be as beautiful. You do lose certain things with certain kinds of visual effects, and you would certainly lose them with AI,” he continued. 

	The brothers were also quizzed about the impact of the Paramount–Warner Bros. merger on filmmakers. 

	“The honest answer is I really don’t know how that’s all going to shake out. And I don’t know enough about the politics between who’s owning what,” Joel said, laughing nervously when he was pressed about the merger. “I do know that, obviously, the more all these companies are consolidated into one or two companies, or three companies, that’s not good. Because competition is what drives the market, but it’s also what produces opportunities for different kinds of movies.” On Paramount leadership, specifically, he said, “I don’t know about David Ellison.”

schema.headline: Joel Coen Talks Studio Consolidation –  ‘Competition Is What Produces Opportunities for Different Kinds of Movies’ – and Teases Reunion Film With Brother Ethan

title: J.K. Rowling’s Agent Slams Trans Rights Protest at ‘Harry Potter and the Cursed Child’ in London: It Put ‘Others at Risk’
description: J.K. Rowling’s agent Neil Blair has slammed the transgender rights activists who staged a dramatic protest before a gala performance of “Harry Pott
body:
J.K. Rowling’s agent Neil Blair has slammed the transgender rights activists who staged a dramatic protest before a gala performance of “Harry Potter and the Cursed Child” on Thursday in London’s West End.

	The protesters, many wearing masks, hats and goggles to hide their identity, stormed the red carpet as celebrities were arriving for a new shortened version of the show at the Palace Theatre. The activists, one with a T-shirt stating “Rowling money kills,” lay on the red carpet before they were dragged off by security guards.
	

	In a statement provided to Variety, Blair said, “We respect peaceful activism and the right to express different views. But those rights must be exercised without putting others at risk, including audience members, performers and theater staff, as we saw [Thursday] evening during the protests outside the Palace Theatre in London ahead of the gala performance of ‘Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.'”


	He added, “Above all, we want to continue bringing the magic of Harry Potter to the wonderful fans who have supported and embraced this world for so many years. Every fan deserves to enjoy the magic of Harry Potter in an atmosphere of respect and security, and we remain committed to keeping live theater a welcoming and safe experience for everyone.”

	Local celebrities in attendance for the special performance included TV hosts Vanessa Feltz, Angellica Bell and Richard Arnold, and “The Chase” star Anne Hegerty.

	The show, originally in two parts, has been reconfigured to become a single-part performance lasting almost three hours.
	

	Rowling has been vocal in her criticism of self-declared gender identity, and this has led to allegations that she is transphobic, which she has strongly denied. She has previously said she respects “every trans person’s right to live any way that feels authentic and comfortable to them.”

	In a statement sent to Variety by the Guild of Angry Transsexuals, a group that claimed to have organized the protest, one of the protestors, Thea, said, “We took action to make attendees of Rowling’s ‘Cursed Child’ [aware] that by continuing to fund her media and entertainment empire, they directly fund the legal attack on trans people, their rights and private lives.”

schema.headline: J.K. Rowling’s Agent Slams Trans Rights Protest at ‘Harry Potter and the Cursed Child’ in London: It Put ‘Others at Risk’

title: Taylor Swift Heroine Clara Bow’s Breakout Movie ‘It’ Leads Carlotta Films, Artcraft Pictures French Distribution Deal of Hollywood Classics
description: LYON, France — “It,” the 1927 breakout movie of silent film star Clara Bow, to whom Taylor Swift paid tribute in a song named after her in “The Tor
body:
LYON, France — “It,” the 1927 breakout movie of silent film star Clara Bow, to whom Taylor Swift paid tribute in a song named after her in “The Tortured Poets Department,” leads a deal between French classic film distributor Carlotta Films and U.S. restoration company Artcraft Pictures.

	Under the terms of the deal, Carlotta will represent its Artcraft’s catalogue across all rights in France, bringing a collection of Hollywood classics from the silent and early sound eras to French theaters and home entertainment.
	

	The collaboration is being launched at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival with a newly restored version of Clarence G. Badger’s “It” (1927), the romantic comedy that propelled Clara Bow to stardom and established her as Hollywood’s original “It girl.” The film will screen Oct. 17 at Lyon’s Auditorium, accompanied on the organ by Italian musician Gabriele Agrimonti.


	Bow also inspired Margot Robbie’s character Nellie LaRoy in Damien Chazelle’s “Babylon.”

	Other titles covered by the agreement include Herbert Brenon’s “Beau Geste” (1926), starring Ronald Colman; Cecil B. DeMille’s “The Affairs of Anatol” (1921), starring Gloria Swanson; and William C. deMille’s “Miss Lulu Bett,” adapted from Zona Gale’s Pulitzer Prize-winning play. The slate also extends to early sound films, including Lionel Barrymore’s “His Glorious Night” (1929), starring John Gilbert.

	Artcraft Pictures was founded by two American film preservation specialists: James Mockoski, a longtime archivist and restoration expert who worked with Francis Ford Coppola’s American Zoetrope, and Robert A. Harris, whose work with James C. Katz includes landmark restorations of David Lean’s “Lawrence of Arabia,” George Cukor’s “My Fair Lady” and Alfred Hitchcock’s “Vertigo.”
	

	The company takes its name from the original Artcraft Pictures, a distribution banner established in 1916 that became part of Paramount Pictures and was associated with some of the studio’s biggest silent-era stars, including Mary Pickford.

	“Artcraft Pictures is thrilled to join Carlotta Films. We share a passion for keeping cinema’s roots alive so new fans can enjoy them,” said Mockoski. “So many wonderful classics could easily fade away, but together with Carlotta, we’re making sure that never happens.”

	Artcraft is also working with the San Francisco Silent Film Festival, which began collaborating with Mockoski and Harris in 2025 on restorations from Paramount’s silent-era library. The restored “Beau Geste” was presented at the Telluride Film Festival earlier this year.

	For Carlotta, which has spent close to three decades distributing classic cinema in France, the agreement expands a catalogue that already includes major works of the silent era, from F.W. Murnau’s “Sunrise” and films by Frank Borzage and Erich von Stroheim to G.W. Pabst’s “Pandora’s Box,” starring Louise Brooks.

	Carlotta plans to release the films in France theatrically and on Blu-ray, with individual release dates yet to be announced.

	“We’re delighted to represent Artcraft in France and introduce audiences to its restorations of both celebrated and lesser-known American silent films,” said Carlotta’s Vincent Paul-Boncour. “It’s a pleasure to work with James Mockoski and Robert Harris, two seasoned experts in film history and restoration, and to launch this collaboration with the French premiere of the beautifully restored ‘It.’”

	The MIFC wrapped in Lyon on Oct. 16. The Lumière Film Festival runs through Oct. 18.

schema.headline: Taylor Swift Heroine Clara Bow’s Breakout Movie ‘It’ Leads Carlotta Films, Artcraft Pictures French Distribution Deal of Hollywood Classics

title: ‘Renoir’ Producers Join Asia-Europe Co-Production Panel at Tokyo Market as Japanese Accelerator Atmovie Global Track Partners With Ties That Bind
description: Producers behind Hayakawa Chie’s Cannes competition title “Renoir” are among the speakers at a session on Asia-Europe co-production at Tokyo’s TIFF
body:
Producers behind Hayakawa Chie’s Cannes competition title “Renoir” are among the speakers at a session on Asia-Europe co-production at Tokyo’s TIFFCOM market on Oct. 30, as Japanese accelerator Atmovie Global Track formalizes a partnership with Europe-based workshop Ties That Bind.

	The open panel, titled “Building Creative Partnerships,” will examine how producers and directors work together to bring projects up to an international level, drawing on case studies of films made between the two regions. It will run in tandem with the Tokyo International Film Festival, and any TIFFCOM badge holder can attend. 
	

	On the panel are Mizuno-Gray Eiko, CEO of Tokyo-based Loaded Films, and French producer Christophe Bruncher of Ici et Là Productions, who both worked on “Renoir,” which competed at Cannes in 2025. Mizuno-Gray’s credits also include Hayakawa’s “Plan 75,” which received a special mention for the Caméra d’Or at Cannes in 2022 and went on to become Japan’s Oscar entry, as well as Kurosawa Kiyoshi’s “To the Ends of the Earth.” She is developing a Poland-Japan co-production from director Ishikawa Kei and a Japan-Philippines project from Hirayanagi Atsuko, and is also a support producer on the accelerator. She also sits on the Tokyo festival’s Asian Future jury this year.


	Bruncher, a La Fémis graduate who speaks Mandarin, is head of studies for Ties That Bind. His recent co-productions include Muriel d’Ansembourg’s Berlinale title “Truly Naked” and Kamila Andini’s Toronto selection “Four Seasons in Java,” both of which feature at this year’s Tokyo festival.
	

	Joining them are Oh Heejung, the Seoul- and Amsterdam-based founder of Seesaw Pictures, whose films have played Sundance, Berlin, Locarno, IDFA, Rotterdam and Busan, and Moriya Takeshi, the Atmovie CEO who founded the accelerator. Moriya’s producing credits span TV series “Midnight Diner” and Uchida Eiji’s “Midnight Swan,” which was named picture of the year at the 44th Japan Academy Film Prizes. Atmovie Global Track producer Sekiguchi Mio, whose credits include Uchida’s “Fiamma,” curated the panel.

	Ahead of the public event, Oh and Bruncher will mentor a closed two-day workshop for the accelerator’s fellows on Oct. 27 and 28, built around group sessions in which participants will develop their projects and discuss career paths rather than sit through lectures. 

	The overall program was curated by Alessandro Gropplero, who runs the Friuli Venezia Giulia Audiovisual Fund and co-founded Ties That Bind, which the FVG fund organizes with EAVE and the Udine Far East Film Festival. The workshop brings European and Asian producers together on project development, financing, co-production opportunities and networking.

	Atmovie Global Track prepares Japanese filmmakers to take original projects into the international co-production market through lectures and mentoring from Japanese and overseas industry figures. Selected fellows pitch at festivals, with milestones including the Japan Pavilion at Cannes in May 2025 and the Japan Pitch event at the Busan International Film Festival in October. The organizers said many creators struggle to build trust across cultures and to communicate outside their native language, and that the open session is meant to share lessons with the wider industry and grow the network of Japanese filmmakers pursuing international work.

	Support for the program comes from the Japan Creator Support Fund, which the Japan Arts Council created using Agency for Cultural Affairs funding.

schema.headline: ‘Renoir’ Producers Join Asia-Europe Co-Production Panel at Tokyo Market as Japanese Accelerator Atmovie Global Track Partners With Ties That Bind

title: Miley Cyrus Embraces Being the Anti-Pop Pop Star With Her First ‘Bass Persuades’ Concert at Hollywood Bowl: Concert Review
description: After she descended from a B-stage in the middle of the stands at the Hollywood Bowl on Friday night, Miley Cyrus sat hunched over on the main stag
body:
After she descended from a B-stage in the middle of the stands at the Hollywood Bowl on Friday night, Miley Cyrus sat hunched over on the main stage, visibly sapped by the 200-foot trek back to the spotlight. “You guys gave me so much energy, but you also took a little energy out of me, too,” she said. “It is a lot for me, if you could imagine walking from where I was through each of you and feeling how much passion and how much love each of you radiates to me. And I appreciate you so much. But it is a lot for me and it is a little bit overwhelming.”
	

	It’s an admission that a seasoned pop star — one of our biggest and brightest, mind you — would rarely deign to make at their first major show in years. And yet, it felt like the thesis for the first of two concerts Cyrus is performing in Los Angeles in support of her latest album “Bass Persuades,” a record with a few bright moments but lacking the singular vision that defined some of her strongest work. Across the nearly two-hour set, Cyrus appeared at odds with the pressures of being a generational talent, proudly chasing her muse with full-throated renditions of fresher, more opaque material while letting the audience carry the vocals on her biggest hits. It was confounding, oftentimes bizarre and, in the end, strangely entertaining, a snapshot of a megastar who, after all this time, is still figuring out what artist she wants to become.


	That’s the thrill for anyone who has followed Cyrus’ career since she emerged as a Disney star with “Hannah Montana,” trying on different styles while navigating the mercurial sound of mainstream pop. She’s shape-shifted at a moment’s notice, chasing massive hits with pivots into deeply unconventional genres and sounds, beginning with her reinventive “Bangerz” era in 2013 and its subsequent global trek, her last extensive tour. Since then, she’s remained prolific and expansive, traipsing from psych-pop (“Miley Cyrus & Her Dead Petz”) to glam rock (“Plastic Hearts”) and, perhaps not accidentally, stumbling into a few massive hits along the way, with songs like “Wrecking Ball” and “Flowers” that she let the audience carry during the Bowl show.
	


	On Friday night, Cyrus hewed closely to her new material with tracks from “Bass Persuades” and a few from 2025’s wildly ambitious “Something Beautiful.” She’s performed so rarely that nearly half the songs on the setlist were live debuts: Over the past few years, Cyrus staged only two fans-only shows in Los Angeles and Paris, appearances that reinforced her strengths as a performer without heeding to the pressures — interviews, TV appearances, radio drops — that come with it.

	Yet Cyrus was quick to ground the show in her reality, one where she’s learned to balance her public and private lives. “For somebody that likes to keep life fun, and likes to jump out of airplanes and be spontaneous, doing the same thing for your entire life can lose its shine if you don’t continue to give yourself that pressure and polish to create something beautiful, which is the life that I’m living,” she said, leading into the title track from “Something Beautiful.”

	For Cyrus, that’s meant stretching the boundaries of pop music and, by proxy, pop stardom. All bets were off as she opened with “Orbit,” a very languid ballad about the magnetism of romance. Already the pace was unpredictable, giving way to the zapping synth-pop of “Different Religion” (with featuring and opening act Model/Actriz) and Fentanyl-rejecting “Bass Persuades.” She let her freak flag fly with Flaming Lips’ frontman Wayne Coyne on the B stage for the group’s “Do You Realize??” and their collaboration “Karen Don’t Be Sad,” and strutted across the catwalk at the lip of the stage for “Walk of Fame,” one of the more supermodel songs in her discography.

	Amid her musings on fame, she struck a truly emotive moment in remembrance of her godmother Dolly Parton, recalling that the only time she had seen her perform was at the Bowl some years back. “Like so many things Dolly did that I didn’t understand at the time, sitting here with you all right now, feeling her all around me, knowing that she’s right here beside me every day, all the time, more than she could be when she was here, I feel her more than ever,” she said, choking back tears as she led into a cover of “Jolene.” “And knowing that I get to share this story with you all, it makes that night very worth it. This memory is gold to me. Me and Dolly, we are eternal. Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart. And I’m going to see her again, and I can’t fucking wait because I miss her.”
	


	That’s where she felt most at home, belting out those familiar notes of “Jolene” as she’s done so many times before. So it was strange that she largely held the mic towards the crowd for her bigger hits, “We Can’t Stop” and “Party in the U.S.A.,” where Coyne reemerged with a gigantic assortment of balloons that spelled “Fuck Yeah Hollywood Bowl.” Cyrus seemed removed from those tracks, aware of the power they held over the attending crowd while recognizing they had become so woven into the cultural fabric that they no longer belonged just to her.

	Perhaps that’s why the first of Cyrus’ shows at the Hollywood Bowl felt so possessive, so intrinsically tied to her recent eras and willing to explore them. There were no traditional dance breaks or wild set pieces to accent the songs; here was Cyrus, 33 years old, coming out on the other end of the hit factory with the freedom to be who she’s meant to be. Whether that’s satisfactory is of little significance when, across two sold-out nights, 18,000 fans are still pining to witness it.

schema.headline: Miley Cyrus Embraces Being the Anti-Pop Pop Star With Her First ‘Bass Persuades’ Concert at Hollywood Bowl: Concert Review

title: Coen Brothers Bring Laughs to Lumière Award Ceremony as Javier Bardem Recalls ‘No Country for Old Men’: ‘They Gave Me One Masterpiece’
description: To the sound of the Gipsy Kings’ Spanish-language rendition of “Hotel California,” Joel and Ethan Coen took the stage at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festiv
body:
To the sound of the Gipsy Kings’ Spanish-language rendition of “Hotel California,” Joel and Ethan Coen took the stage at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival on Friday evening to receive the Lumière Award, celebrating four decades of filmmaking with a characteristically irreverent tribute to the inventors of cinema.

	“Thank you to the Lumières for inventing the movie camera, or we’d have been fucked,” joked Ethan, drawing laughs from the audience.
	

	The musical choice itself was a nod to the Coens’ cult comedy “The Big Lebowski,” featuring John Turturro’s flamboyant bowler Jesus Quintana.


	The star-studded gathering included Javier Bardem, Frances McDormand, former Lumière prize winner Wim Wenders, Robert Eggers, Michel Hazanavicius and Bérénice Bejo, Benoît Magimel, Antoine de Caunes and Caleb Deschanel, in town for a masterclass and the premiere of Laika’s upcoming stop-motion animated feature “Wildwood.”

	Accepting the award, Joel reflected on four decades of filmmaking with his brother. “We did it because we love cinema and we love storytelling,” he said. “We’ve had, pretty much with certain exceptions, nothing but fun making these films over the decades.”

	Bardem, who won an Oscar for his chilling portrayal of Anton Chigurh in “No Country for Old Men,” delivered one of the evening’s most colorful tributes, recalling how he initially tried to turn down the role despite being a longtime admirer of the Coens.

	“I sat down with them in New York in their office and I was like, ‘Listen, I admire you, I worship you, you are amazing, but I hate violence, I don’t drive, and I can barely speak English. What the hell am I doing here?’” Bardem recalled.
	

	“They gave me no reason whatsoever to do the movie. They were just laughing,” he said. “I thought, ‘I don’t know what this experience is going to be like, but I know it’s not going to be stressful. So yes, let’s fucking do it.’”

	Bardem also joked about his character’s infamous haircut, which the Coens had spotted in a photograph from the 1960s. “I was single at the time – this is 2006 – and I said, ‘I’m gonna be single until the day I wrap.’”

	Ethan had another story about Bardem’s commitment to the role. The actor had decided his character needed to be pale, he recalled, so during the largely outdoor shoot, a young production assistant would accompany him to the set holding a light blue parasol over his head. “And he wonders why we laughed at him,” Ethan joked.

	The actor’s tribute took a more heartfelt turn as he reflected on what working with the brothers had meant to him. “What they gave me was one masterpiece and the gift of a lifetime, personally and professionally,” Bardem said. “They made a dream come true. Ten years after me saying that would never happen, it happened. And it was even better than I would have ever imagined.”

	The evening also featured musical tributes, with French singer-songwriter Bénabar performing Charles Aznavour’s “Parce que tu crois,” chosen by Joel Coen as his favorite song. Five-time Grammy winner Angélique Kidjo delivered a rendition of Jacques Brel’s “Ne me quitte pas,” one of Bardem’s favorites.

	Festival director Thierry Frémaux drew laughs by projecting photographs of the Lumière and Coen brothers striking remarkably similar poses, before reminding the filmmakers that, in keeping with festival tradition, they would have to shoot their own version of the Lumières’ first film, “Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory,” on Saturday. After screening one of the original versions, he gave them until the next day to come up with their own take.

	The tribute also struck a timely note with the screening of Ettore Scola’s 1997 short “1943-1997,” which follows a young Jewish boy fleeing a Nazi roundup in wartime Rome who finds refuge in a movie theater. As five decades of Italian cinema unfold on screen, the boy grows old. The film ends in 1997 with a young African boy fleeing persecution into the same theater, drawing a parallel between past and present.
	

	Bardem picked up on the film’s message, stressing its relevance today. “Never again is never again for everybody, from Congo to Sudan to Palestine,” he said.

	Joel also paid tribute to Lyon’s community of film lovers and the festival’s commitment to the shared experience of cinema, praising audiences who still relish “gathering in a dark room with lots of other people and seeing it on a big screen.”

	Since making their feature debut with the neo-noir thriller “Blood Simple” in 1984, Joel and Ethan Coen have built one of American cinema’s most distinctive filmographies, spanning the crime comedy “Raising Arizona,” cult favorite “The Big Lebowski,” Depression-era musical odyssey “O Brother, Where Art Thou?” and Western anthology “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs.”

	Their 2007 thriller “No Country for Old Men” won four Oscars, including best picture, best director, best adapted screenplay and best supporting actor for Bardem, while “Fargo” earned the brothers their first Oscar for original screenplay in 1997.



	

									Olivier CHASSIGNOLE
	



	At Cannes, their remarkable run began in 1991 when “Barton Fink” swept the Palme d’Or, best director and best actor prize for John Turturro. They went on to win best director for “Fargo” in 1996 and “The Man Who Wasn’t There” in 2001, while “Inside Llewyn Davis” took the Grand Prix in 2013. In 2015, they returned to the Croisette as presidents of the festival’s jury.

	Friday’s honor makes Joel and Ethan the second filmmaking duo to receive the Lumière Award, following Belgian brothers Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne in 2020. Previous recipients include Clint Eastwood, Quentin Tarantino, Pedro Almodóvar, Martin Scorsese, Catherine Deneuve, Wong Kar-wai, Jane Fonda, Francis Ford Coppola, Jane Campion, Tim Burton, Wim Wenders, Isabelle Huppert and Michael Mann.

	The Lumière Film Festival wraps Sunday, Oct. 18.

schema.headline: Coen Brothers Bring Laughs to Lumière Award Ceremony as Javier Bardem Recalls ‘No Country for Old Men’: ‘They Gave Me One Masterpiece’

title: Pathé Unveils Sofia Coppola’s ‘Marie Antoinette’ 4K Restoration as Sophie and Jérôme Seydoux Are Feted in Lyon
description: Sofia Coppola’s cult classic “Marie Antoinette” and three works by Louis Daquin, a champion of the Communist Resistance during the German occupatio
body:
Sofia Coppola’s cult classic “Marie Antoinette” and three works by Louis Daquin, a champion of the Communist Resistance during the German occupation, are among the latest restored works from French studio Pathé.

	The company, whose owners Jérôme Seydoux and Sophie Seydoux are being honored at the Lumière Film Festival’s International Classic Film Market (MIFC) in Lyon, is celebrating its 130th anniversary this year, which also marks the 20th anniversary of the Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé Fondation. 
	

	A bastion of film preservation and the continued transmission of heritage works, Pathé has also been a strong supporter of the Lumière Festival since its establishment in 2009. 


	The studio is currently marking the 20th anniversary of Coppola’s film with the release of a newly restored 4K version on Nov. 25.

	The film, which stars Kirsten Dunst and Jason Schwartzman, comes just in time for the recently announced special exhibition at the Chateau de Versailles dedicated to the movie.

	The 4K restoration is being supervised by Sony Pictures Entertainment in collaboration with American Zoetrope. It follows the late Eleanor Coppola’s new documentary on her daughter’s film, “Making Marie Antoinette.”

	Pathé is also celebrating the work of Daquin, described by the Lumière Festival as “a unique figure in French cinema, for whom filmmaking and political commitment were one and the same. A member of the Resistance, a staunch communist and union activist heavily involved in defending film industry workers, he considered his craft to be an extension of his convictions.”
	



	

					Nous les gosses (Portrait of Innocence)
									Courtesy of Pathé Films
	



	Part of a special Lumière Festival showcase, Daquin’s works include his 1941 film “Nous les gosses”(“Portrait of Innocence”), the story of a close-knit group of schoolchildren that can be read as a veiled call for resistance. The fest is presenting the film in its restored 2K version.

	Likewise screening is 1960’s “The Opportunists” (“Les Arrivistes”), an adaptation of Honoré de Balzac’s book “La Rabouilleuse” (known in English as “The Black Sheep” and “The Two Brothers”); set during the Restoration, it follows a former officer of Napoleon whose greed knows no bounds.



	

					The Opportunists (Les Arrivistes)
									Courtesy of Pathé Films – DEFA Spielfilmstudio
	



	The Lumière Festival will present the film in its restored 4K version.

	Also in the Pathé catalogue is the 4K restoration of Daquin’s 1944 drama “Premier de Cordée” (“First in Line”). Filmed primarily on location in the Chamonix Valley, “Premier de Cordée” represented a remarkable technical achievement during the German occupation of France, Pathé notes.

	“Directed by a filmmaker involved in the Resistance, the film tells the story of a young man who must overcome his fear of heights to become a mountain guide. Its themes of struggle, perseverance and self-transcendence resonated strongly with audiences in occupied France.”

	Pathé describes the Daquin showcase as “an opportunity to rediscover a filmmaker who captured working-class France, made films under the very nose of the occupying forces, and helped shape the institutions of post-war French cinema.

	“Louis Daquin’s career was extraordinary. He directed several feature films during the German occupation while actively involved in the Communist Resistance. His films from this period bear the mark of this paradoxal situation: a left-wing filmmaker, involved in the Resistance, working under the constraints of a fascist regime.”

	Speaking at the Pathé Bellecour theater in Lyon during the Classic Film Market on Friday, Jérôme Seydoux, chairman of Pathé, and Sophie Seydoux, president of the Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé Fondation, discussed a wide range of pressing issues, from their efforts to preserve, conserve and transmit the company’s century-long heritage to the resilience of cinema, the undeniable power of blockbusters, and the importance of education in cultivating a lasting passion for cinema among young people.
	

	Pathé has produced such recent upscale blockbusters as “De Gaulle: Résistance,” “The Count of Monte Cristo” and “The Three Musketeers – Part I: D’Artagnan” — the kinds of films that are necessary to keep cinema alive, according to Jérôme Seydoux.

	“It is essential that there are films that are called locomotives in France, which Americans call blockbusters. .We at Pathé said to ourselves that we are not going to make cars, we are going to make locomotives. But it’s difficult. It’s difficult because these are obviously bigger risks. These are often bigger budgets. So, you can’t make too many mistakes.”

	Citing a motto from filmmaker Claude Berri, Jérôme Seydoux added, “When making a film, what matters is not what it costs, it’s what it brings in.”

	Expressing his confidence in the survival of cinema, the Pathé chairman argued that despite recurring economic crises, technological shifts and the rise of home viewing, people would always seek the shared emotional experience of the big screen.

	“That cinema is something that would disappear has been said since the Lumière Brothers. The Lumière Brothers, Jean-Pierre Melville, the head of Netflix, and more recently, Sylvester Stallone have announced that the cinema does not exist anymore.

	“Cinema will resist, no matter what happens,” he stressed. “Cinema has always had crises. There will always be cinema, there will always be crises. And why will there always be cinema? Because today, in a society where people are very individualistic, they still have, at some point, the need to come together, to share emotions together. I am an absolutely unshakeable believer in the survival of cinema.”

	Cinema will not only resist the dominance of U.S. streamers in France, it is sure to become a significant venue for platforms to launch their productions, Jérôme Seydoux added. The U.S. streamers are also natural partners for Pathé, he stressed. 

	“Today in France, the two main networks for the French are YouTube and Netflix. So these are two American companies. And we are going to work almost automatically with people who have money. The people who have money are the platforms. So yes, we will definitely work with the platforms. It’s mandatory.”
	

	At the same time, Netflix will increasingly release films in theaters, he predicted. “I think they will discover that they need, what I call high fashion. When you are in the media business, you need something that shines.” For that reason, “in a short time, in a few years Netflix will make movies that will be released in theaters.”

	“Not just because of the talents involved, but also for commercial reasons, for reasons that if you want to do something that is truly an event, it is difficult to make an event only on television. It will always be an event whose notoriety will be lower than that of a major film event.”

	Turning to the company’s film preservation efforts and the use of digital technology, Sophie Seydoux stressed the importance of maintaining film on film.

	“I am an unconditional supporter of what is called a conservation shoot, meaning that once we have restored a film, digitized it, it goes back to film. We know from here at the Lumière Festival, everywhere in the world, film is preserved for 120 years in an absolutely remarkable way. Currently, for everything that is digital, we do not know the preservation time. And above all, there are a lot of elements that can disappear overnight due to a change in technology. So, we need to be very, very careful.

	“At Pathé, it’s really a golden rule. We reprint on film for all the restorations we do. There is never the slightest shadow of hesitation about it.”

	Sophie Seydoux also underscored the importance of education and exposing children to films from an early age to cultivate a lasting passion for cinema. The Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé Foundation conducts specialized educational workshops centered around silent films.

	“It is very, very, very important to show young people films from early childhood because it will give them this desire to continue to see films,” she said. “At the Foundation we have a very, very important educational program that is focused on silent films, since that is our specialty. We teach them what film is, we let them handle film. Handling is something that is very important.

	“[Company founder] Charles Pathé was very attached to everything that was manipulation. He thought about it when he built a camera, about the cameraman’s gestures, how it should be done, how it could be improved. And manipulation is very important, so many of our workshops for children involve hands-on activities.”



	

					Sophie Seydoux and Jérôme Seydoux
									Courtesy of MIFC/Bertrand Rindoff/Getty

title: ‘Trust Me, I’m a Doctor’ Review: Kal Penn and Abbie Cornish Star in a Minor Sidebar to the Anna Nicole Smith Story
description: Andy Warhol famously said that in the future, everyone will have 15 minutes of fame. “Trust Me, I’m A Doctor” expands that tally to an hour and 51
body:
Andy Warhol famously said that in the future, everyone will have 15 minutes of fame. “Trust Me, I’m A Doctor” expands that tally to an hour and 51 minutes for Sandeep Kapoor, the physician who treated Playboy Playmate Anna Nicole Smith and was implicated in her death from a prescription drug overdose in 2007. That’s too long.

	Though it’s difficult to chronicle any element of Smith’s life without injecting at least a hint of tabloid sensationalism, writer-director Thane Economou (“The Wedding Party”) takes an aggressively cheeky approach to the saga of Kapoor’s involvement, in the process undercutting what he clearly intends to be an empathetic portrait of both the doctor and his patient. Taking the lead in a rare film focused on a prominent Indian American, Kal Penn struggles to wrangle this flamboyant biopic into a serious acting challenge, but he delivers impressive work in its final scenes even if they fail to elevate what came before them.
	

	Penn plays Kapoor, a closeted physician who takes over a retiring colleague’s practice, in the process inheriting Anna Nicole Smith (Abbie Cornish) as a patient. Like his predecessor, Sandeep agrees to treat Smith under a pseudonym, but she quickly beguiles him with her childlike charm; despite his attempts to maintain a professional distance, he soon becomes a part of her inner circle. Shortly after she invites him to ride in a Los Angeles Pride parade where he participates in a self-described “orgy,” Anna announces that she’s pregnant — with whose baby, he does not know. Even so, he determines that failing to prescribe methadone to curb her festering drug addiction could harm her pregnancy, so he reluctantly writes a big order for her to take with her on a weeks-long trip to the Bahamas.
	

	She eventually gives birth to a daughter, Dannielynn, and just three days later, loses her son Daniel (Jordan Kronis) to an overdose. A few months later, Sandeep learns from news reports that Anna herself has overdosed; he rushes to his office to confiscate her and Daniel’s medical files to protect them from being stolen or leaked, but the media has already staked out his practice. At the urging of a devoted patient, Margie (Jocelyne Zucco), he retains no-nonsense attorney Ellen Garofalo (Linda Hamilton) and mounts a PR campaign to present himself as the upstanding medical professional he claims to be. But when federal investigators discover Anna’s medical records in his underwear drawer, he becomes an official suspect in her death.

	Eventually, the attorney general working at the direction of gubernatorial hopeful Jerry Brown charges Sandeep, along with Smith’s lawyer Howard K. Stern (David Julian Hirsh) and her psychiatrist Khristine Eroshevich (Virginia Cowan), of criminal conspiracy, with him as the lead plaintiff. As he fights to clear his name, Sandeep unexpectedly discovers that his best ally to win the case may be Harvey Levin (Elon Gold), the TMZ journalist whose photos first incriminated him, even as he reckons with the cost of his relationship with Smith on his family, his practice and his future.

	According to this film, Sandeep Kapoor was kind of a nitwit regarding his time in the spotlight, but he ultimately occupied only a marginal place in Anna Nicole Smith’s story. His famous patient passes away 25 minutes into the film; the remaining 86 minutes focus on Garofalo’s legal maneuverings and his own incredulity at virtually every part of the process of being put through the public wringer.

	Given Smith’s celebrity status and the sensational ups and downs of her life, it’s easy for an audience unfamiliar with Kapoor’s memoir, which inspired the film, to assume that he was a sycophant and enabler of this troubled woman. Economou seems to want to do justice to both his and his patient’s lives, but his script obfuscates Kapoor’s involvement in her death more than necessary by jumping back and forth in time, peppering what was already intriguing subject matter with fourth-wall-breaking monologues, montages that meld real and staged footage and at least one sidebar about a character who, though objectively interesting, is more or less totally irrelevant to this story.
	

	Events such as his interview with Levin — as Garofalo’s legal strategy or his personal leap into the belly of the media beast — are especially fascinating when we see actual footage of their conversation over the closing credits. But they are unfortunately sandwiched between reams of expository commentary about each participant’s real and imagined motivations, political undertones of the lawsuit brought against him, and Kapoor’s only semi-convincing protestations of his innocence. 

	Understandably, Penn struggles to hold these disparate points of focus together with a performance that vacillates between disarmingly dopey and almost willfully ignorant of the realities of the 2000s media landscape. It does not help that, outside of Hamilton as his tough-as-nails defense lawyer, the rest of the performances are delivered at an almost parodic pitch, led by Cornish with a rendition of Smith that seems pitched more to “Saturday Night Live” than a real film for the big screen.

	All of which is to say “Trust Me, I’m A Doctor” probably would have worked better as a documentary than as a narrative feature. Even taking Kapoor at his word that he never wanted and was happy to recede afterward from the public eye, Economou clearly possesses an impressive enough archive of material to tell this story with or without his participation, with the same multimedia flair that he deploys here. If nothing else, moviegoers wouldn’t have had to watch Cornish play Smith, an admittedly unenviable acting tightrope that she navigates clumsily at best. Kapoor, meanwhile, seems much more self-possessed in the real footage, making him precisely as sympathetic as the filmmaker intended.

	Following a handful of genuinely powerful scenes by Penn that sadly come too late to offset the circus-like tone established earlier, the film concludes with a montage detailing what happened to everyone involved after the verdict was handed down in Kapoor’s case. The overarching message of that sequence is that something about celebrity worship seems to drive people crazy, imagining anything connected to it as more significant than it actually is. With respect to Kapoor, Economou should have paid more attention to the epiphanies of his own film; the rollercoaster of Smith’s life will always be a curio, but that doesn’t mean that every passenger on it has a story worth telling.

title: Harry Styles Performs New Song, Tribute to Liam Payne on Anniversary of His Death
description:

body:
Harry Styles
                          Honors Liam Payne With New Song ...
                          On Anniversary Of His Death

                              October 17, 2026
                            7:05 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Harry Styles paid tribute in a big way to Liam Payne during his Friday night gig at Madison Square Garden, belting out a special song he wrote in memory of his late former bandmate.
      
    
            Styles hit the stage at MSG in Midtown Manhattan for his latest performance Friday and to showcase his yet-to-be-released song, “What Is Enough," which Harry specifically wrote for Liam.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            As you know, the two were very close when they were members of the famous boy band, "One Direction," along with Niall Horan, Louis Tomlinson, and Zayn Malik.
      

            What made the moment even more poignant during Harry's MSG concert was that it marked the anniversary of Liam's untimely death. In October 2024, Liam fell to his death from a third-floor balcony at a hotel in Buenos Aires, Argentina.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Before diving into the new song, Harry took a moment to talk to the sold-out crowd about Liam, saying that two years ago today he lost one of his closest friends.
      
    
            Harry continued ... “I’m sure a lot of you have been through similar things. I hope you haven’t. But really, it’s just about looking after each other.”
      
    
            He went on ... “So many people who have touched my life in such special ways. I wouldn’t be here without. I’m gonna play you a song I wrote for my friend about two years ago, if that’s all right.”
      
    
            Then Harry brought down the house with his live rendition of “What Is Enough,” honoring his late friend as the crowd went wild.

title: Pope Leo Will Be Released From Hospital Today After Lung Cancer Surgery
description:
Pope Leo XIV
                          Set To Be Released From Hospital After Lung Cancer Surgery
body:
Pope Leo XIV
                          Set To Be Released From Hospital After Lung Cancer Surgery ...
                          Time To Give Some Blessings!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 17, 2026
                            5:46 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 17, 2026
                                6:44 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
          UPDATE
  
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            6:42 AM PT -- Pope Leo XIV was just spotted walking out of Gemelli Hospital in Italy, with a big security detail around him ... as a massive crowd wished him well just outside the front doors.
      
    
            Good news for Pope Leo XIV ... the pontiff is set to be released Saturday from the hospital after a four-day stay during which he received lung cancer surgery, according to the Vatican.
      
    
            The Vatican also announced that the Pope won't miss out on his traditional Sunday blessing from St. Peter’s Square.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As you know, the 71-year-old Leo had surgery on his right lung after doctors spotted what appeared to be a cancerous nodule. During the procedure, doctors confirmed it was adenocarcinoma, a very common lung cancer.
      

            Leo's personal physician and surgeon gave the pope the green light to be released, saying he was "fit for discharge from the hospital” based on blood test results and a chest X-ray, as well as an assessment of his clinical condition.
      
    
            According to the Vatican, Leo will exit the hospital in the early afternoon to return to St. Peter's Square for Sunday's blessing ceremony.
      
    
            Thank God!!!

title: Casey Anthony Calls to Abolish the Death Penalty
description:
Casey Anthony
                          Death To Capital Punishment!!!
body:
Casey Anthony
                          Death To Capital Punishment!!!
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Casey Anthony says America needs to do away with the death penalty ... 15 years after she narrowly avoided the punishment herself.
      
    
            Casey -- who was found not guilty of murdering her 2-year-old daughter Caylee back in the summer of 2011 -- says state-sanctioned death as a punishment is inhumane ... claiming there's no evidence that the severe punishment stops people from committing crimes.
      
    
            She mentions how 17 inmates have already been executed in Florida this year ... and 19 were killed in the Sunshine State in 2025.
      

            Casey points out the economic cost of death penalty trials and executions as another reason to do away with the punishment. She also argues the burden of proof should remain on prosecutors ... and it shouldn't fall on defense attorneys to have to explain why their client doesn't deserve to die while simultaneously fighting for their freedom.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She finishes off her post by seemingly reflecting on her own experiences ... writing, "What if the person you are condemning to death is innocent?"
      
    
            As you know ... Florida prosecutors were seeking the death penalty during Casey's murder trial -- and, if she had been found guilty, it's possible she would've been sentenced to die.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The death penalty has been a major topic of conversation in recent weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike ... which landed the convicted killer in a Tennessee hospital.
      
    
            She spent nearly 2 weeks in the hospital before she was released.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            In addition, Nidal Hasan -- the former U.S. Army Major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood -- will soon be executed by firing squad ... which officials first claimed they planned to live stream before Trump reversed course.
      
    
            Bottom line ... executions are getting a lot of attention in the USA -- and Casey says it's time to kill the practice.
